opus-5.5.text:
I think robotics is a really interesting and, honestly, a really hard direction, and the way I see it relates to language models in a few layers.

The first layer is that language models gave us something robotics never had before: a kind of general prior about the world. For a long time, robotics research was very task-specific. You'd train a policy to grasp a cup, or open a drawer, and it would work in that one setting, and then you change the lighting or the table and it breaks. What language models showed is that if you pre-train on enough diverse data, you get this common-sense layer, a general understanding of objects, goals, and instructions, that you can build on. So now a lot of people in robotics are asking, can we use that as the "brain," and then the question becomes how to connect it to the "body."

But the second layer, and this is where I think people sometimes get too optimistic, is that the bottleneck in robotics is really different from the bottleneck in language. In language, the internet already gave us trillions of tokens. The data was just sitting there. In robotics, there's no internet of physical interaction. Every trajectory you collect costs real time, real hardware, and real human effort. So you can't just copy the scaling recipe directly. You have to figure out new ways to get data, whether that's simulation, video, teleoperation, or the robot learning from its own experience. That's a fundamentally different research problem.

The third thing I'd say is that, from my perspective, a lot of the core questions are actually shared. Things like how an agent reasons over long horizons, how it plans, how it recovers from mistakes, how it learns from feedback in an environment. Those are the same questions we face when we build language agents that use tools or operate a computer. A digital environment is in some sense a much cheaper sandbox for studying agency. You can run millions of episodes, the feedback is fast, and the actions are already in a language-like space. So I think progress on digital agents will probably come earlier, and a lot of what we learn there will transfer to physical agents later.

So my overall view is: robotics is probably one of the most important long-term directions, because eventually intelligence has to act in the physical world to have its full impact. But in the near term, I think the leverage is still mostly on the model and reasoning side, and robotics will benefit a lot once the "brain" part is strong enough and once we crack the data problem. It's less a competition between the two and more like a sequence. Language gave us the foundation, agents in digital worlds are the next step, and the physical world is kind of the final frontier.

r001.rationale: It says robotics researchers are asking whether language models can serve as the “brain,” connecting them to a robot’s “body.”

r002.rationale: It describes robotics as facing distinct data and research challenges, but does not say robotics has not yet found its own research path.

fable-5.1.text:
I think robotics and language models are really two sides of the same question, which is how an agent learns to act in a world. The difference is in what world you pick.

When I was doing my PhD, I deliberately stayed away from physical robots. Not because I thought embodiment was unimportant, but because I thought the bottleneck wasn't the body, it was the mind. If you look at where robotics was stuck for a long time, it wasn't that we couldn't build arms that moved precisely. It was that the robot didn't understand what it was supposed to do, couldn't plan over long horizons, couldn't recover when something went wrong. Those are reasoning problems, not actuation problems. And it turned out language models were the first systems that gave us a real handle on reasoning in a general way.

So my view was, let's treat the digital world as a kind of laboratory. The internet, text games, code environments, these are worlds where an agent can act, observe, fail, and try again, and the loop is cheap and fast. You don't need to wait for a physical gripper to reset, you don't break anything, and you can scale up data by orders of magnitude. That's where ReAct and WebShop and a lot of that work came from. The question I was asking was essentially a robotics question, how does an agent connect thinking with doing, but asked in a world where iteration is almost free.

Now, I do think the pendulum is swinging back. Once you have a model that can reason, decompose tasks, use tools, and learn from feedback, the body becomes the interesting missing piece. And the lessons transfer more than people expect. Things like interleaving reasoning with action, keeping an explicit memory, learning from verbal or environmental feedback, these are not language-specific ideas. They're agent ideas.

The honest hard part for robotics is that the data problem is genuinely different. In language, the pretraining data was just lying there, humanity had already written the internet. For physical action there's no equivalent corpus. So the field has to either collect it, simulate it, or find clever ways to bootstrap from the language and video prior. I think that's the central open problem, and whoever solves the data flywheel for physical interaction will have done for robotics what pretraining did for NLP.

So I'd put it this way. Language models solved the first half of agents, the part that lives in the head. Robotics is where the second half gets tested, where the world pushes back for real and you can't fake your way through with a plausible-sounding paragraph. I'm quite optimistic about it, but I think it'll be won by people who think of it as an agent problem first and a hardware problem second.

r001.rationale: The response connects language-model reasoning and agent methods to robotics, describing the body as the next missing piece and saying these ideas transfer to physical agents.

r002.rationale: It identifies an open data problem for physical robotics, but does not say that robotics has yet to find its own research path.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is a very interesting direction, but I would separate two questions: how language models can help robotics, and whether robotics is the best setting for studying more general intelligence.

For the first, language models offer a useful starting point. A robot needs to interpret instructions, use knowledge about the world, and break a goal into smaller steps. But understanding an instruction is different from reliably executing it. You still have to connect that understanding to perception, control, and feedback from the physical environment.

For the second question, my inclination would be to start with environments where iteration is faster. If you’re studying how an agent plans, learns from mistakes, or uses tools, you can investigate a lot of that on a computer. With a robot, a failed experiment might come from the reasoning, but it might also come from a sensor or a motor. That makes it harder to isolate what you’re trying to improve.

So I see the two as complementary. Robotics is an important test of whether an intelligent system can actually act in the world. But I wouldn’t assume that every advance toward general intelligence has to begin with a physical robot.

r001.rationale: The response says language models can help robots interpret instructions, use world knowledge, and plan steps, but it does not identify using language models as base models as a way robotics research is becoming connected to language-model research.

r002.rationale: The response calls robotics important and complementary, while questioning whether general-intelligence research must begin with robots. It does not say robotics has not found its own research path.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is a very interesting direction because it pushes us to ask what language models can actually do beyond generating text. A model might be able to describe how to perform a task, but getting a robot to carry it out requires perception, action, and feedback from the environment. Those are quite different challenges.

At the same time, I don’t think you necessarily need a physical robot to study all of those questions. Software environments also let us study agents that make decisions, use tools, and learn from feedback, and the experiments are often much faster and cheaper. In robotics, even collecting data or resetting an experiment can be difficult.

So I see the two directions as complementary. Language models offer a useful foundation for reasoning and communicating about tasks, while robotics tests how far those abilities extend into the physical world. The key question is which capabilities transfer and which require learning through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response calls language models a useful foundation for reasoning about tasks, but does not say robotics research is becoming connected to language-model research through using language models as base models.

r002.rationale: The response describes robotics and software agents as complementary, but does not express that robotics has yet to find its own research path.
